name: Saga
intent: Keep data consistent across several services without a global transaction, by running a sequence of local steps and undoing completed ones with compensating actions if a later step fails.
scenario: Booking a trip needs three separate services: reserve a flight, reserve a hotel, and charge the card. Each service owns its own database, so no single transaction can cover all three.
problem: In a single database a transaction can roll everything back. Across services there is no shared transaction. If the flight and hotel are reserved but the payment is declined, the system is left half-done: seats and rooms held for a customer who will never pay.

howItWorks.title: Break the job into local transactions
howItWorks.text: Each step (reserve flight, reserve hotel, charge card) is an ordinary transaction inside one service. It commits immediately and its effects become visible.

howItWorks.title: Every step has a compensating action
howItWorks.text: For each step there is a way to semantically undo it: cancel the flight reservation, release the hotel room, refund the payment. Compensation is a new action, not a database rollback.

howItWorks.title: On failure, run the compensations in reverse
howItWorks.text: If charging the card fails, the saga cancels the hotel and then the flight, in reverse order, until the system is back in a consistent state. A step that failed itself needs no undo.

howItWorks.title: Orchestration or choreography
howItWorks.text: With orchestration a central coordinator tells each service what to do next and decides when to compensate. With choreography each service reacts to the previous service's events and publishes its own, with no coordinator. Orchestration is easier to follow; choreography has fewer moving parts but is harder to see as a whole.

howItWorks.title: Steps must be retryable and durable
howItWorks.text: Messages can be duplicated or delayed, and the coordinator can crash. Steps and compensations must be idempotent, and the saga's progress is persisted so it can resume. Some actions cannot be truly undone (an email already sent), so order steps with the hardest-to-undo ones last.

pros: Consistency across services without distributed locks or two-phase commit
Each service keeps its own database and stays independent
Failures are handled explicitly and recoverably
Works with asynchronous messaging, so no long blocking calls
cons: Only eventual consistency: other users can see intermediate states
Compensating actions must be designed and tested for every step
Hard to reason about, and hard to debug across services
No isolation: concurrent sagas can interfere with each other
whenToUse: A business process spans several services, each with its own data store
Two-phase commit is unavailable or too costly
Each step can be reasonably undone or compensated
whenNotToUse: All the data lives in one database that supports ACID transactions: use one
A step cannot be compensated and its failure would be unrecoverable
The process is so simple that one service could simply own all of it
pitfalls: Compensations that are not idempotent, or that themselves can fail without retry
Treating a compensation as an exact inverse when it is really a business decision (a refund fee)
Showing users a half-finished state, such as a hotel 'booked' that is later cancelled
Choreography that grows into an unreadable web of events

roles.label: Orchestrator
roles.description: Runs the steps and triggers compensation.

roles.label: Service
roles.description: Performs one local transaction and can undo it.
